title: Agreements that ran past their first end date
question: Which agreements now end later than first agreed, by how many months, and are they still being paid years past the first end date?
finding: Both a first and a latest end date can be read for 454 agreements. 252 now end a year or more after the first date and 199 two years or more; the typical extension among the 252 is 30 months. 178 of them read as more years at about the same yearly cost and 66 as more years at a higher yearly cost. The longest: Motorola Solutions Inc (Emergency Management), first due to end 2027-11-30 and now running to 2038-11-30. Where the agreement can be found in the payment file, 114 were still being paid two or more fiscal years after the first end date.
how: Board of Supervisors titles from 2014 to 2026 were linked into one record per agreement, following only links proven by a dollar figure carried from one title to the next or by a shared contract number (the rule used in the amendment-growth screen). The first amount is the total in the first approval on file or, where the first file is an amendment, the amount that amendment says it started from; the latest is the highest total approved. Left out: 527 leases and property; 225 no usable name in the title; 167 agreements with other public bodies; 164 no amount in any title; 58 loans; 21 agreements that bring money in (concessions, rents, franchises). The first end date is the earliest end the titles give: the end stated in the first approval, or the end an amendment says it is extending from, or, failing both, the end as it stood at the first amendment on file (which understates the extension). The latest is the latest end any title gives. Months over is the difference. "Last paid" is the last fiscal year with payments on the matching contract (matched by the City contract number where the title prints one, otherwise by the same party and a ceiling within 2% of the latest Board figure); blank means no match.
limits: An agreement written with options to extend can run past its first end date, and the City often extends a service rather than interrupt it while a new competition is run. For services the question is whether the work was offered to anyone else before it was extended, which the titles do not say. For a project with a fixed scope, such as design or construction management, a later end date usually means the project itself is late. Dates are text-mined and each row links to its file. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
